pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10 000 000 and determine the value of each digit.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.A.2 (read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare with >, =, <) extended by 5.NBT place value; CCSS does not name a 10,000,000 ceiling explicitly.
• Operational details: Group digits into three-digit PERIODS (ones, thousands, millions) separated by commas/spaces; read each period as a three-digit number followed by its period name. Stress that the comma structure, not the raw digit count, drives reading. Handle placeholder zeros within and between periods (7,045,200). Order by scanning from the most significant digit; align by periods.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write 4,302,561 in words.' Tier B: 'State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200.' Tier C: 'Order four seven-digit numbers and justify using the leading digits.'
bestPractices: Teach reading by three-digit periods (ones/thousands/millions): read the period as a 3-digit number, then say its name — the comma grouping is the reading tool
Foreground internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (7,045,200) as the main difficulty; require the child to hold empty places
Order by a most-significant-digit-first scan with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time
Move fluently between numeral, words and expanded form, and value-of-a-digit statements ('the 7 is worth seven million')
Use real 7-digit contexts (populations, distances, view counts) so magnitude is meaningful, not just symbol-copying
keyRepresentations: Period-grouped place-value chart with Millions | Thousands | Ones panels
Three-pane translator: numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded form
Number line / magnitude bar for ordering seven-digit values
commonMisconceptions: Misreading placeholder zeros — reading 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred forty-five thousand two hundred' by dropping empty places
Losing period boundaries and reading digit-by-digit for very large numbers
Confusing face value with place value (the 7 as 'seven' not 'seven million')
Assuming more digits always means larger without aligning periods when digit counts match
Inserting or omitting 'and' / mis-segmenting when writing in words

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: read, write, order and compare whole numbers up to 10,000,000 and state the value of each digit. The core difficulty is the three-digit PERIOD structure (ones, thousands, millions) and holding placeholder zeros (e.g. 7,045,200). Learners should build numbers, translate fluently between numeral, words and expanded form, state digit values as place value (the 7 in 7,045,200 is 'seven million'), and order by a most-significant-digit-first scan with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time.

activities.title: Period builder with live three-way echo
feedback: If the words and the numeral stop corresponding (e.g. reading 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred forty-five thousand two hundred' by dropping the internal zero), rebuild in the period-labelled grid and read each three-digit group, then attach its period name.

If a digit's value is misnamed (e.g. the 7 as 'seven' or 'seven hundred thousand'), count columns from the right in threes to find the period, or read the whole number aloud so the 7 is heard as 'seven million'.
Point out explicitly that the internal zero in 7,045,200 is doing a job: it holds a place even though it is not spoken.
activities.rationale: A live builder that groups digits into periods and simultaneously echoes numeral, words and expanded form is intended to make the period structure and placeholder-zero handling operative as the child constructs numbers, rather than only described. Linked numeral/words/expanded panels and live recomputation are optional interaction examples that make the reading mechanism concrete. The cited standards describe the content and the numeral/number-name/expanded-form representations being practised; they are not evidence that this interaction is more effective than another medium.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
4.NBT.A.2: read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare using >, =, <.
learnerActions: Set each digit onto a place-value chart labelled Millions | Thousands | Ones, grouped into three-digit periods.

As each digit is placed, watch the number appear three ways at once: the comma-grouped numeral (e.g. 7,045,200), the words read period by period ('seven million, forty-five thousand, two hundred'), and the expanded form.

Deliberately build numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (e.g. set the hundred-thousands place — the leading digit of the thousands period — to 0, as in 7,045,200) and observe how the words panel skips the empty place without dropping the period boundary.
State aloud, for a chosen digit, its full place value (e.g. 'the 7 is worth seven million').
activities.intendedInsight: The comma/period grouping — not the raw digit count — is what lets you read a large number aloud; each nonzero three-digit period is read as a number then given its period name (the ones period has no spoken name, and a period that is all zeros, as in 7,000,200, is skipped entirely), and an internal zero silently holds a column without being spoken.

activities.title: Write, value and order on paper (consolidation)
feedback: If ordering is done by length or first digit only, align the numbers vertically by place and compare digit by digit; with equal leading digits, keep comparing rightward until a difference appears — here 3,204,000 and 3,240,000 agree until the ten-thousands digit (0 vs 4) within the thousands period.
After writing in words, re-check the period breaks: 'How did you know where to put the comma/period breaks?'
Probe the placeholder zero: 'What is the value of the 0 in 7,045,200 — does it do anything?' and extend with 'Write the number that is one more than 4,302,561 in words.'
activities.rationale: These read/write/value/order tasks are directly assessable and consolidate the notation-heavy procedure. The near-identical ordering set (same leading digits, differing in the thousands period) discriminates place-by-place comparison from shortcuts like length or first digit. These are proposed consolidation tasks, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
learnerActions: Write 4,302,561 in words (answer: four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one).
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 (answer: seven million).
For the ordering, align the numbers by place and compare left-to-right, moving right only when digits tie; say which digit finally decided between 3,204,000 and 3,240,000.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing, valuing and ordering seven-digit numbers all rely on the same period structure and on place-by-place comparison, including when leading digits agree.

activities.title: Labelled reference number with tap-to-reveal periods
feedback: If a learner relies only on this fixed example, move them to constructing their own numbers so they practise assembling arbitrary values and resolving orderings themselves.
activities.rationale: A fixed, labelled example with tap-to-reveal period names and digit values is a useful reference anchor; it supports recognition and recall but does not by itself require the learner to assemble arbitrary numbers or resolve orderings. Pair it with build/write tasks.
learnerActions: Study a labelled seven-digit number (e.g. 4,302,561) and tap each three-digit period to reveal its name and read-out.
Tap an individual digit to reveal its place value.
Use this as a reference anchor while writing or ordering other numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly period-labelled example makes the millions/thousands/ones structure and per-digit place values visible as a stable reference.

activities.title: Dictation and 'why isn't the zero spoken?' discussion
feedback: If the dictated number is written with wrong grouping (especially around an internal zero), rebuild it in the period grid and align each spoken group to a period.
Prompt the learner to justify comma/period placement rather than count digits.
activities.rationale: Spoken dictation plus responsive discussion can probe the reasoning behind placeholder zeros and period breaks; it may complement, rather than replace, interactive construction of the notation. This is a proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Listen to a mentor dictate a large number in words and write it as a comma-grouped numeral.
Explain why a placeholder zero (e.g. in 7,045,200) is not spoken yet must still be written.
Discuss how the comma/period breaks map to the spoken words.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why an internal zero holds a place without being spoken is intended to support and strengthen the learner's grasp of the period structure.

constraints: Target objective: read, write, order and compare whole numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine each digit's value, including numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros.
State digit values as place value (e.g. 'seven million'), not face value ('seven').
Order by scanning most-significant-digit-first with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time; do not order by digit count or first digit alone when lengths/leading digits match.

The tap-to-reveal labelled number is a reference scaffold: it supports recognition but does not elicit independent construction of arbitrary numbers or ordering decisions; pair it with build/write tasks. This is a narrow affordance limit, not a claim that reference examples cannot teach.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. multiple-choice value-of-digit) can assess but do not by themselves require the learner to construct words or resolve an ordering; include production tasks (writing in words, assembling numbers, ordering).
Use real seven-digit contexts (populations, distances, view counts) so magnitude is meaningful rather than symbol-copying.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the UK DfE National Curriculum claim as verified=true and the CCSS 4.NBT.A.2 claim as verified=false; retained as provided without re-checking.
The source observes that CCSS does not explicitly name a 10,000,000 ceiling; the upper bound comes from the UK Y6 standard. Treated as a scope note, not a universal claim.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'poor' and framed a quiz as only a 'co-consolidator'; these are catalog fit judgements, not pedagogical laws, and have been expressed as affordance/limit statements rather than claims that any medium cannot teach.

The original correct answer writes 'three hundred two thousand' without 'and'; UK convention often inserts 'and' (e.g. 'three hundred and two thousand, five hundred and sixty-one'). Retained as given; the pedagogy notes mis-insertion/omission of 'and' as a known writing error.

The curriculum source claims attached to the builder activity support the content and representations (numeral/number name/expanded form), not the effectiveness of the interactive medium; efficacy wording is kept conservative throughout.

probeDeeper: How did you know where to put the commas when writing it in words?
What is the value of the 0 in 7,045,200 — does it do anything?
For the ordering, which digit finally decided between 3,204,000 and 3,240,000?
Write me the number that is one more than 4,302,561 in words.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one. (2) seven million. (3) 3,024,000; 3,204,000; 3,240,000; 3,420,000.

errorPatterns.pattern: Period/grouping error — misreads 4,302,561 (e.g. 'four hundred thirty thousand...') or writes it as digits with wrong grouping, especially around the internal zero.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the number in a period-labelled place-value grid (millions | thousands | ones); read each three-digit group then attach its period name.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Words and digits do not correspond; the millions or thousands period is mislabelled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place when valuing a digit — gives the 7 in 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred thousand' or just 'seven'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count columns from the right in threes to name the period, or read the whole number aloud so the 7 is heard as 'seven million'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digit value is off by one or more powers of ten; child counts columns unreliably.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by length or first digit only — with equal leading digits, compares wrongly or guesses, ignoring later place values.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align the numbers vertically by place and compare left-to-right digit by digit, moving right only when digits tie.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ordering breaks on the near-identical numbers; child stops comparing once early digits match.

responseLevels.gap: Misgroups periods, misvalues digits by powers of ten, or orders by length/first digit.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes, values and orders seven-digit numbers reliably, using period structure and left-to-right place comparison, including numbers with internal zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most seven-digit numbers but stumbles on internal zeros or on comparing numbers that agree in the leading digits.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Three tasks on paper. (1) Write 4,302,561 in words. (2) State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200. (3) Order these smallest to largest: 3,240,000; 3,204,000; 3,024,000; 3,420,000.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch how the child handles the periods and the internal zeros. Reading to millions requires grouping digits into millions/thousands/ones periods and holding placeholder zeros; the near-identical ordering set (same leading digits, differing in the thousands period) exposes whether comparison is done place-by-place or by a shortcut like length or first digit.
